subject: snailfish
title: A Fish Was Filmed 27,349 Feet Down, Deeper Than Any Other

scenes.text: There's a depth where fish stop existing. One lives right there.
Cameras in a trench off Japan caught a baby snailfish swimming.
Eight thousand three hundred thirty-six meters down. Over five miles.
The water presses more than eight hundred times harder than at the surface.
Why no deeper? Fish need a molecule that shields their proteins from pressure. Past about eight thousand four hundred meters, they likely can't make enough.
So this tiny fish is swimming at the floor for every fish on Earth.

description:
A juvenile snailfish was filmed 8,336 meters (27,349 feet) down in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench off Japan, the deepest fish ever recorded on camera.
Researchers think fish can't live much below 8,200 to 8,400 meters, because they can no longer make enough TMAO, a compound that protects their proteins from the pressure.
What do you think lives below the fish limit?
first_comment: Snailfish have no swim bladder, which is part of why they handle the pressure. They feed on tiny crustaceans in the trench. Below this depth, the bottom belongs to shrimp-like amphipods and worms. Would you ride a sub down there?
